clue.text: Tasteless stuff by current film-maker

parts.note: tat is cheap, tasteless goods or junk
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A critic sneers that a director's work sits beside a lot of trashy tat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like an adjective meaning modern, but it is the electrical quantity. Jacques Tati was a French comic film director (Monsieur Hulot's Holiday).
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Tati directed and starred in classic French comedies, so he is an example of a film director.

clue.text: Hover in quiet to first-class Asian city

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, splitting the outer letters

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
to hang in the air is to hover
A1 means first-class, with the 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A drone hovers quietly before heading off to a first-class Asian destination.
explanation.walkthrough: The hovering goes inside the call for quiet, splitting it. A1 is read with the digit as the letter I, a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Shanghai is China's largest city, a major port on the Yangtze delta, so it is an Asian city.

clue.text: Adores holding first of annual bloomers?

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: to adore is to love

indicators.note: the first of a word means only its opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of annual

explanation.surface: A gardener dotes on flowers that bloom each year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' looks like flowering plants (or knickers), but a bloomer is a British crusty loaf with diagonal slashes on top; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a type of large bread loaf in Britain, so bloomers are examples of loaves.

clue.text: Old apartment beginning to erode recently

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
a flat is the British word for an apartment

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of erode

explanation.surface: An old apartment block has lately started to crumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to erode' reads as a verb phrase about decay, but it just supplies an E.
explanation.definitionFit: Of late is an adverbial idiom meaning in the recent past, a direct equivalent for recently.

clue.text: Code of silence newcomer tackles somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat means only to a degree, so just part of the following text is used

parts.note: found running across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A new recruit to the mob partly confronts its rule of silence.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of newcomer into the start of tackles.
explanation.definitionFit: Omerta is the Mafia rule forbidding members from talking to police, literally their vow of silence.

clue.text: Secure part of Barnet?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to fasten shut with a key
second meaning: a strand of hair, Barnet being slang for hair

explanation.walkthrough: Barnet looks like the London borough, but in Cockney rhyming slang 'Barnet Fair' means hair, so a part of one's barnet is a tress of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for making something fastened and a noun for a single tress or curl of hair.

clue.text: Deserter playing truant holds firm

indicators.note: to hold is to keep within, so one piece goes inside the other
playing about suggests messing around, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging
Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A soldier who skips duty stands firm, or perhaps a truant clings to a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like an adjective meaning steadfast, but it is a noun for a company.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat is someone who switches sides or abandons their party, a figurative deserter.

clue.text: Place for cleaning club jumper in centre of Richmond

parts.note: a bat is a club used in cricket or baseball

indicators.note: something put in another is enclosed by it
the centre of a word is its middle, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of this eight-letter name
a roo, short for kangaroo, is a jumper

explanation.surface: Someone launders a club sweater at a cleaners in Richmond, a London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is the British word for a sweater, which suits the cleaning picture, but here it is a kangaroo. ROO sits between H and M.
explanation.definitionFit: A bathroom is the room where people wash themselves, so it is a place for cleaning up.

clue.text: Accompany Charlie in unusual store

indicators.note: placed in means set inside the other letters
something unusual is out of its normal form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone takes a friend named Charlie along to an unusual shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie reads as a person's name, but it is the radio code word for C.
explanation.definitionFit: To escort someone is to go along with them as a companion or guard, a synonym for accompany.

clue.text: Formally transfer Italian gentleman touring outskirts of Venice

indicators.note: touring means going all around something, so one piece encircles another

parts.note: signor is the Italian title for a gentleman, Mr

indicators.note: outskirts are the edges, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of Venice

explanation.surface: An Italian gentleman tours the edges of Venice before handing over a deed.
explanation.walkthrough: The touring signor wraps around VE, splitting before his final R.
explanation.definitionFit: To sign over property is to transfer its ownership legally by signing a document.

clue.text: Roguish demonstration without leader

indicators.note: having no leader means the front letter is dropped

parts.note: a protest march is a demonstration

explanation.surface: A cheeky protest goes ahead with nobody leading it.
explanation.walkthrough: MARCH loses its first letter. 'Arch' as an adjective is a slightly old-fashioned word for playfully mischievous.
explanation.definitionFit: An arch look or remark is knowingly mischievous and teasing, which matches a playful, cheeky sense of roguish.

clue.text: Worked out child finally gave in study

indicators.note: placed in means set inside the other letters

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university
a son is a child

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of gave

explanation.surface: A child finally gave in during homework after working the problem out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gave in' looks like surrender, but 'gave' is split off for its last letter and 'in' is the container signal. To read a subject is British usage for studying it.
explanation.definitionFit: To reason something out is to work it out by logical thinking, so reasoned matches worked out.

clue.text: Card game's fashionable still?

parts.note: snap is a children's card game, with the possessive giving the S
hot means trendy or fashionable

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a certain card game is still in fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' reads as an adverb meaning yet, but it is a noun: a still photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: A snapshot is a quick informal photograph, and a still is a single photographic image, so it is an example.

clue.text: Love nightlife in London primarily

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Someone mainly loves the nightlife in London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' looks like a verb, but it is the score of zero in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis scoring love means zero, and nil is the word for zero in football scores.

clue.text: Testing second electronic device with Heather

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for second
an amp, short for amplifier, is an electronic device
ling is another name for common heather

explanation.surface: Someone tests a second gadget alongside a woman called Heather.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather is capitalised to look like a name, but it is the moorland plant, also called ling.
explanation.definitionFit: Sampling means trying a small portion to judge quality, a direct synonym for testing.

clue.text: Mother to fix mature plant

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
to rig a result is to fix it dishonestly
old means mature in years

explanation.surface: Mum sets out to repot a fully grown plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix' fits the gardening picture as planting firmly, but it is the sense of fixing a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: The marigold is a common garden flower with orange or yellow blooms, an example of a plant.

clue.text: Most ancient poem contains line on saint

indicators.note: to contain is to have within, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
l is the abbreviation for line
St is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: The earliest surviving poem includes a line about a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed below, so ST comes after the poem holding its line.
explanation.definitionFit: Oldest is the superlative of old, meaning the most aged, and so equivalent to most ancient.

clue.text: Oddball yelped intensely

indicators.note: an oddball is eccentric and out of the ordinary, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: An eccentric person let out a loud, intense cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddball' looks like the subject of the sentence, a strange person, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling something deeply means feeling it profoundly or strongly, a synonym of intensely.

clue.text: Silent Greek character extremely tiresome

parts.note: mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its ends, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of tiresome

explanation.surface: A quiet Greek person turns out to be terribly dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person in a story, but here it is a letter of an alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Mute describes someone not speaking or making no sound, which is to be silent.

clue.text: Cover over open-air swimming-pool

parts.note: a lid is a cover
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Pool staff pull a cover over the outdoor swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as a preposition, but it is the cricket term for a set of six balls, abbreviated O.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a lido is a public outdoor pool, originally named after the Venice beach resort.

clue.text: Director-general keeping healthy in house

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: DG is the abbreviation for director-general
to be well is to be healthy
taken as written

explanation.surface: A senior executive stays fit while working from home.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in' is not a link word: it is letters kept inside the abbreviation alongside healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: A dwelling is any place where someone lives, so a house is a dwelling.

clue.text: Perhaps a fixture at Burns Night, Anne helps regularly

definitions.text: Perhaps a fixture at Burns Night

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: At a Burns Night supper Anne regularly lends a hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns Night is the Scottish celebration of poet Robert Burns each January, where haggis is served with neeps (mashed turnip or swede) and tatties.
explanation.definitionFit: Neeps are the traditional mashed turnip side dish served with haggis, so one is a fixture of the meal.

clue.text: Complete set of books found in Republic of Ireland

indicators.note: something found in a place lies within it

parts.note: Eire is the Irish-language name of the Republic of Ireland
NT is the New Testament, a set of biblical books

explanation.surface: A full collection of books turns up somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complete set' wants to be one phrase, but 'Complete' alone is the definition and 'set of books' is the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Entire means whole, with nothing missing, which is the adjective sense of complete.

clue.text: US writer, one among anglers at sea

indicators.note: to be among others is to be surrounded by them
being at sea means confused and lost, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An American author joins a party of fishermen out on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' completes the fishing picture, but it is the signal to scramble the anglers.
explanation.definitionFit: J.D. Salinger was the American novelist who wrote The Catcher in the Rye, an example of a US author.

clue.text: Skilful piece of publicity trio broadcast

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, is a piece of publicity

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so these letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A clever advertisement by a singing trio goes out on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the advertising picture as airing on TV, but here it means scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: Adroit describes someone clever or deft with hands or mind, a synonym of skilful.
